title: What AI Romantic Companions Can Never Replace
gist: Sibley and Garcia argue AI romantic companions deliver a 'reassurance revolution' but cannot supply commitment, which drives relationship security. Nearly 1 in 4 US respondents have interacted with romance-simulating AI and about 1 in 7 partnered emerging adults use AI companions regularly, a pattern linked to poorer communication and lower stability.

insights.claim: In a national US sample (Brian Willoughby and colleagues), nearly 1 in 4 reported interacting with AI chat technologies designed to simulate romantic partners.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Sizes a large and growing AI companionship market.
insights.quote: nearly 1 in 4 reported interacting with AI chat technologies designed to simulate romantic partners

insights.claim: About 1 in 7 emerging adults who are dating, engaged or married report regularly interacting with AI romantic companions.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Usage extends into partnered users, not just the lonely single.

insights.claim: AI companions represent a 'reassurance revolution', offering always-on, non-judgmental validation especially attractive to people with loneliness, social anxiety or attachment insecurity.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Explains product-market fit and engagement drivers for AI companion apps.
insights.quote: In many ways, AI companions represent a reassurance revolution.

insights.claim: The authors distinguish reassurance ('Am I okay right now?') from security ('Can I count on this relationship in the future?'), arguing AI can supply the first but not the second.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Defines the ceiling on AI companionship as a substitute for human relationships.
insights.quote: An AI companion can simulate commitment. A human partner can actually commit.

insights.claim: A study led by Samantha Joel and Paul Eastwick with 84 other researchers found perceived partner commitment to be one of the strongest predictors of relationship satisfaction.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Grounds the commitment argument in large-scale evidence.

insights.claim: For attachment-insecure users, reassurance without genuine commitment may trap them in a cycle of validation-seeking rather than building lasting security.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Potential harm vector that could attract regulatory or reputational scrutiny for AI companion products.
insights.quote: reassurance without genuine commitment may leave individuals trapped in a cycle of validation seeking rather than lasting security

themes.theme: Impact on real relationships and family formation

insights.claim: Among emerging adults who were dating, engaged or married, regular AI companion use was associated with poorer communication and lower relationship stability, and many users preferred talking to their AI over their partner (correlational).
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Early evidence AI companions may compete with human relationships; second-order risk to family formation.
insights.quote: Many users also reported preferring conversations with their AI companion to conversations with their real-life partner.

insights.claim: The authors warn of opportunity costs: AI companions may become comfortable enough that some people stop pursuing real-world relationships altogether, acting as a relationship shortcut.
insights.speaker: D. Scott Sibley and Brooklynn Garcia
insights.so_what: Potential drag on marriage and fertility as AI companionship scales.
insights.quote: What happens if artificial relationships become comfortable enough that some people stop pursuing real-world relationships altogether?
